title: Direct Support
description: Direct support is one of three categories of qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B): wages of employees who directly assist researchers or supervisors.
summary: In the U.S. federal R&D tax credit, direct support is one of three categories of qualified services under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3). It covers wages of employees, such as prototype machinists, research data clerks, and laboratory equipment cleaners, who directly assist researchers or first-line supervisors, but excludes supervision and general administrative services.

body.text: In the U.S. federal R&D tax credit, direct support is one of three categories of qualified services under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3). It covers wages of employees, such as prototype machinists, research data clerks, and laboratory equipment cleaners, who directly assist researchers or first-line supervisors, but excludes supervision and general administrative services.

Direct Support constitutes one of the three statutory categories of "qualified services" whose employee wages are eligible for the U.S. federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—formally titled the Credit for Increasing Research Activities—under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-2(c)(3). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), Direct Support is defined as services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. While core research wages capture the scientists and engineers resolving technological uncertainty, Direct Support captures the immediate, indispensable technical and operational labor—such as prototype machinists, research data clerks, laboratory equipment cleaners, and technical report typists—required to enable those researchers and their first-line supervisors to execute qualified experimentation.

Capturing Direct Support wages expands a taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs), either through pro rata time allocation under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) or through 100% wage inclusion when an employee's combined qualified services reach the 80% "substantially all" threshold under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2). However, Direct Support is subject to stringent regulatory boundaries that represent a primary focus of Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examinations. Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) excludes all supervisory activities (which must qualify, if at all, as first-line management under § 1.41-2(c)(2)) and excludes general and administrative (G&A) services or other services that benefit research activities only indirectly—such as payroll processing, research expense accounting, general janitorial upkeep, and executive oversight of financial or personnel matters—regardless of whether the administrative personnel are housed within the R&D department or in a separate corporate unit.

items: Form 6765 Section G Effective Date and Scope: While the IRS initially proposed a 2025 rollout during 2024 draft releases, official IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, released February 6, 2026) establish that Section G (Business Component Information)—where Direct Support wages are reported separately in Column 52—is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (including Tax Year 2024 and Tax Year 2025) and becomes mandatory only for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (Tax Year 2026 returns filed in 2027 and beyond). Furthermore, even for tax years beginning after 2025, Section G exempts qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit as well as controlled groups with $1.5 million or less in total QREs and $50 million or less in average annual gross receipts filing original returns, and limits mandatory component-by-component itemization for non-exempt filers to the "80%/Top 50" business components.

Recordkeeping Standards and Time-Tracking Granularity: While contemporaneous project-based time tracking is a strongly recommended audit defense best practice, neither IRC § 6001 nor 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) mandates a specific tracking technology or minute-level logging. Instead, taxpayers must retain records in "sufficiently usable form and detail" to substantiate claimed QREs, and IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) rules permit supported estimation methods when contemporaneous records are unavailable through no fault of the taxpayer and every underlying assumption is factually substantiated.

Pre-Filing IRS Guidance Mechanisms—PFA Versus PLR: First, qualifying Direct Support wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) establishes eligibility for the IRC § 41 tax credit, whereas deductibility or amortization of domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures is governed separately by IRC § 174A (enacted by Public Law 119-21 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024). Second, under Revenue Procedure 2026-1 (Section 6.02) and Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.30.1, the IRS Associate Chief Counsel ordinarily will not issue a PLR on inherently factual questions (such as whether specific employee duties factually support qualified research), making PLRs a vehicle for questions of law. Factual determinations regarding QRE methodologies and IRC § 41 credits prior to return filing are instead addressed through a Large Business and International (LB&I) Pre-Filing Agreement (PFA) under Revenue Procedure 2016-30 (subject to a $181,500 user fee per distinct issue under IRM 4.30.1) or prospectively for documentation sufficiency through a Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreement (RCRA) under Notice 2004-11.

Embedded Financial Impact Calculation: Mathematically, adding $35,000 to a $120,000 base represents a 29.17% increase (or 22.58% of total QREs), whereas an exact 20.00% increase requires $24,000 in Direct Support wages, yielding $144,000 in total QREs.

body.text: 1. Statutory and Regulatory Foundation of Qualified Services
In-House Research Expenses and the Three Pillars of Qualified Services

Under IRC § 41(a)(1), the regular federal research tax credit equals 20% of the excess of a taxpayer's current-year Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) over a statutory base amount, while the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4) provides a 14% credit on current-year QREs exceeding 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (or 6% of current-year QREs under IRC § 41(c)(4)(B) and Form 6765 Line 24 if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three prior taxable years). Under IRC § 41(b)(1), QREs consist of the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" (generally 65% of amounts paid or incurred to non-employees for qualified research under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A), 75% for payments to qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C), or 100% for eligible energy research payments to universities, federal laboratories, or eligible small businesses under § 41(b)(3)(D)) paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(b)(4), for in-house research expenses of startup ventures, the trade or business requirement is treated as satisfied if the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer or a commonly controlled entity.

IRC § 41(b)(2)(A) defines in-house research expenses to encompass three specific expenditure categories: (i) any wages paid or incurred to an employee for "qualified services" performed by such employee, (ii) any amount paid or incurred for supplies (defined in IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) as tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and depreciable property) used in the conduct of qualified research, and (iii) under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research. Among these three categories, employee wages for qualified services typically constitute the largest share of a taxpayer's QRE base.

The first category, Engaging in Qualified Research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)), encompasses the actual conduct of qualified research that satisfies the four-part statutory test of IRC § 41(d)(1)—namely, eligibility for treatment as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (or IRC § 174 as applicable to the tax year), undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation—such as a scientist or engineer directly conducting laboratory experiments, formulating hypotheses, or building and testing experimental prototypes. The second category, Direct Supervision (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)), covers the immediate supervision—strictly limited to first-line management—of qualified research, such as a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments even if that scientist does not physically perform the experiments. Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) states that Direct Supervision "does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) notes, higher-level research executives may only have their wages included to the extent of the specific fraction of time they personally perform actual qualified research or direct first-line supervision. The third category, Direct Support (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)), consists of services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research.

A technical clarification is warranted regarding how these three categories interact for an individual employee. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3), the functional definitions of Direct Supervision and Direct Support are indeed distinct—and § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly specifies that "Direct support does not include supervision". However, an individual employee is not restricted to performing only one category of qualified service during a tax year; under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), an employee may perform a combination of direct research, direct supervision, and direct support, and all hours spent across any combination of the three categories are aggregated when computing the employee's qualified wage allocation and testing for the 80% "substantially all" threshold.
Statutory Definition of Wages Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(D) and Section 3401(a)

To qualify as an in-house research expense—whether via Direct Support, Direct Supervision, or direct conduct—the compensation paid to the employee must meet the statutory definition of "wages" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D). IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i) cross-references IRC § 3401(a), which encompasses taxable remuneration subject to federal income tax withholding as reported on Form W-2, including regular salaries, hourly wages, taxable bonuses, and taxable spreads from the exercise of non-qualified stock options (where qualification is determined by whether the employee performed qualified services during the grant year, while the wage expense is recognized in the exercise year).

Conversely, non-taxable fringe benefits, employer retirement matching contributions, and other amounts not subject to withholding under IRC § 3401(a) are excluded from QRE wages even if paid to an employee performing 100% Direct Support. Additionally, IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(iii) and Form 6765 Section F (Line 42) explicitly prohibit including any wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Tax Credit under IRC § 51(a), and Form 6765 Section C (Line 27) requires reducing the current-year research credit by the portion of any differential wage payment credit from Form 8932 (Line 2) attributable to wages also used to figure the research credit. For self-employed individuals and owner-employees within the meaning of IRC § 401(c)(1), IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii) defines eligible "wages" to include the "earned income" (as defined in IRC § 401(c)(2)) of such employee.
2. Wage Allocation Mechanics and the Substantially All (80%) Rule
Pro Rata Time Allocation Versus the 80% Threshold

Because Direct Support personnel—such as machinists, laboratory technicians, and technical data clerks—frequently split their work hours between R&D support tasks and routine commercial production or general administrative duties, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d) establishes a two-tier mechanism for quantifying claimable QRE wages.

Under the General Pro Rata Allocation Rule (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)), wages paid to or incurred for an employee constitute in-house research expenses only to the extent the wages were paid or incurred for qualified services performed by the employee. When an employee performs both qualified services and non-qualified services during the taxable year, only the amount of wages allocated to the performance of qualified services constitutes an in-house research expense. In the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the qualified wage amount is determined by multiplying the total IRC § 3401(a) wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year by the ratio of: (a) the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of qualified services for the taxpayer (the sum of direct research, direct supervision, and direct support hours) to (b) the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year.

Under the "Substantially All" 80% Rule (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), notwithstanding the general pro rata allocation rule of paragraph (d)(1), if "substantially all" of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i) or (ii) (any combination of engaging in qualified research, direct supervision, or direct support), then the term "qualified services" means 100% ("all") of the services performed by that employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), an employee meets the "substantially all" requirement if and only if the wages allocated (on the basis used for purposes of paragraph (d)(1), i.e., the qualified time ratio) to qualified services constitute at least 80 percent of the total wages paid to or incurred by the taxpayer for the employee during the taxable year. As the IRS ATG emphasizes, this 80% "substantially all" rule for employee wages under § 1.41-2(d)(2) is legally and functionally distinct from the separate 80% "substantially all" requirement applied to a business component's process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6).

To illustrate how individual Direct Support employee wages are calculated under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) and reported on Form 6765 Section G (Columns 50–53), consider a hypothetical manufacturing taxpayer that tracks employee time contemporaneously across 2,000 annual work hours per full-time employee on a single business component (Project Alpha).

In the first case, Hypothetical Employee A (Senior R&D Lab Technician and Machinist—Below 80% Threshold) receives $90,000.00 in annual IRC § 3401(a) W-2 wages across 2,000 total hours worked. During the year, Employee A spends 200 hours (10.0%) engaging directly in qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1) (assisting engineers in running experimental stress tests), 1,100 hours (55.0%) performing qualified Direct Support under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) (machining custom parts for an experimental prototype model and cleaning laboratory test apparatus after runs), and 700 hours (35.0%) performing non-qualified services (calibrating commercial mass-production machinery). Combining the two qualified categories yields 200 + 1,100 = 1,300 qualified hours, or a qualified time ratio of 1,300 ÷ 2,000 = 65.0%. Because 65.0% is below the 80.0% threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), only the pro rata portion qualifies under § 1.41-2(d)(1): $90,000.00 × (200 ÷ 2,000) = $9,000.00 is reported in Form 6765 Section G, Column 50 (Direct research wages), and $90,000.00 × (1,100 ÷ 2,000) = $49,500.00 is reported in Column 52 (Direct support wages), summing to $58,500.00 in Column 53 (Total qualified wages), while the remaining $31,500.00 is excluded.

In the second case, Hypothetical Employee B (Dedicated Prototype Machinist and Test Data Clerk—At or Above 80% Threshold) receives $85,000.00 in annual IRC § 3401(a) W-2 wages across 2,000 total hours worked. Employee B spends 1,680 hours (84.0%) performing qualified Direct Support under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) (fabricating one-off experimental tooling and compiling raw sensor data from prototype test runs) and 320 hours (16.0%) performing non-qualified routine shop inventory and general facility maintenance. Employee B's strict pro rata allocation before applying the "substantially all" rule is $85,000.00 × (1,680 ÷ 2,000) = $71,400.00 (84.0%). Because 84.0% meets or exceeds the 80.0% "substantially all" threshold under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), 100% of Employee B's services during the taxable year are treated as qualified services, allowing the taxpayer to claim the full $85,000.00 as qualified wages in Column 52 and Column 53 (capturing an additional $85,000.00 − $71,400.00 = $13,600.00 above strict pro rata hours).
3. Deconstructing 26 CFR Section 1.41-2(c)(3) and the Functional Nexus Standard
Regulatory Text and Core Stipulations

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(3) defines both the affirmative scope and the explicit exclusions governing Direct Support claims. First, the regulation specifies that the term "direct support" as used in IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) means services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Second, the regulation establishes a strict boundary between support and management: "Direct support does not include supervision. Supervisory services constitute 'qualified services' only to the extent provided in paragraph (c)(2) of this section" (which restricts supervisory qualification strictly to first-line management). Third, the regulation categorically excludes overhead and indirect functions, stating that direct support of research activities "does not include general administrative services, or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities," and specifies that this exclusion applies "whether general administrative personnel are part of the research department or in a separate department".
The Functional Nexus Standard: Proximate Nexus Versus Indirect Benefit

Specifically, the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) confirms that IRC § 41 requires taxpayers to establish a direct link ("nexus") between claimed QREs and specific business components (qualified research activities). For Direct Support wages, this means the employee's service must directly facilitate the specific experimental task performed by the researcher or first-line research supervisor, rather than merely supporting the business organization as a whole. Furthermore, both 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) and the IRS ATG mandate that credit eligibility be determined by the actual functional task performed by the employee during a specific time period. Because 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) denies Direct Support qualification to general administrative personnel even when they are formally assigned to the R&D department, an organizational chart showing that an administrative assistant, financial analyst, or corporate officer reports to the Vice President of R&D does not provide a valid legal defense during an IRS examination. Conversely, an employee housed in a manufacturing or operations department (such as a shop machinist) can perform qualified Direct Support during the specific hours spent fabricating an experimental prototype part for an R&D engineer.

Each of these excluded activities represents a general corporate overhead function that only indirectly benefits research activities. Even when an outside accountant is hired specifically to keep books and records pertaining to a qualified research project (as illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 7, which illustrates the contract research rules of § 1.41-2(e)(1)–(4)), the Treasury Regulations hold that such accounting services do not constitute qualified research under IRC § 41(d) and would not constitute qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) if performed by an employee of the taxpayer, and therefore no portion of the fee constitutes a qualified research expense.

body.text: Evaluating Ambiguous Support Roles: IT Support and Specialized Procurement
In contemporary R&D environments, support functions often extend beyond the traditional regulatory archetypes of typists, clerks, lab cleaners, and machinists.

With respect to Information Technology (IT) Support (analyzed under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)), standard corporate IT functions—such as general network administration, employee workstation provisioning, software license management, and general help-desk troubleshooting—are general and administrative (G&A) services that benefit the enterprise generally and are excluded under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) (consistent with the G&A support services characterization in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) for internal-use software).

With respect to Specialized Technical Procurement (analyzed under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)), general purchasing agents, vendor contract administrators, and supply chain managers perform excluded G&A functions under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3). Nevertheless, because procurement and IT roles sit on the boundary of G&A administration—and the IRS ATG instructs examiners to focus audit scrutiny on employees whose job descriptions suggest administrative or manufacturing duties—any claim for technical procurement or specialized IT support hours requires rigorous, contemporaneous task-level documentation demonstrating that the activity directly assisted the scientist in the experimental process rather than routine purchasing or IT overhead.
4. Substantiation, Recordkeeping, and Form 6765 Section G Reporting
Statutory and Regulatory Recordkeeping Requirements (IRC Section 6001 and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(d))

The legal obligation to substantiate Direct Support wages derives from IRC § 6001, Treasury Regulation § 1.6001-1, and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d). Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) states: "A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

While real-time project-level time tracking with task narratives is the strongest defense against examination adjustments, neither IRC § 41 nor 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) or § 1.41-4(d) legally mandates tracking time down to "minutes" or requires a specific digital timekeeping software. Instead, the IRS RCCATG and IRS ATG Section 7 establish four core evidentiary principles governing examination review.

First, regarding Project-Based Accounting Versus Cost Centers, while IRC § 41 does not mandate a single accounting system, project-based accounting is strongly preferred over cost-center or hybrid approaches because it captures costs directly at the business component level and establishes the required nexus between QREs and qualified research activities. Cost-center accounting accumulates expenditures by department without evaluating whether underlying activities satisfy IRC § 41, and hybrid methods that multiply departmental W-2 pools by broad subject matter expert (SME) percentage estimates frequently fail to establish an auditable nexus between accounting records and specific research activities. Second, regarding Rejection of Unverified or Arbitrary Estimates, the IRS is not required to accept estimates of QREs if documentation exists to verify the actual amount of such expenses, and claims resting solely on arbitrary percentage estimates or unsupported cost-center allocations justify partial or complete disallowance.

Third, under the Judicial Standard for Estimation Methods summarized in IRS ATG Section 7, courts allow an estimation method only when the taxpayer lacks contemporaneous records and where the sole issue is the exact amount paid or incurred in the qualified research activity, and only if two prerequisites are met: (a) the taxpayer first establishes that it engaged in qualified research activities as defined in IRC § 41(d), and (b) the failure to maintain a proper system to capture relevant information is not an "inexactitude... of their own making". Even when permitted, taxpayers must possess factual support for every assumption underlying their estimates to meet their burden of proof, which may be corroborated by contemporaneous project artifacts—such as lab notebooks, work orders, project authorizations, budgets, prototype build logs, progress reports, and meeting minutes—alongside credible oral testimony from technical and supervisory personnel with personal knowledge. Fourth, with respect to Notices of Inadequate Records, pursuant to 26 CFR § 1.6001-1(d), if a taxpayer fails to keep sufficient or adequate records supporting the research credit claimed, IRS examiners are instructed to consider issuing a formal Notice of Inadequate Records, specifically Letter 978 (DO) (Notice of Inadequate Records), Letter 979 (DO) (Inadequate Record Notice), or Letter 1022 (DO) (Inadequate Records Notice Follow-up).
Navigating the Redesigned IRS Form 6765 and Section G

First, with respect to Effective Dates, the final Instructions for Form 6765 explicitly provide that for tax years beginning before 2026 (which includes both Tax Year 2024 and Tax Year 2025), completing Section G is optional for all filers (unless filing an amended return). Taxpayers who choose not to complete Section G for a pre-2026 tax year (or who are exempt from completing Section G) check "No" on Question A of Section F and enter their total in-house wages for qualified services across all business components directly on Section F, Line 42. Completing Section G becomes required only for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (i.e., Tax Year 2026 returns filed in 2027 and subsequent tax years), and even then is subject to explicit small-taxpayer exemptions.

Second, with respect to Exemptions from Section G, even for tax years beginning after 2025, a taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G on an original return if it meets either of two statutory or administrative criteria. Under the Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Credit Exemption, the taxpayer is exempt if it is a QSB as defined under IRC § 41(h)(3)—a corporation (including an S corporation), partnership, or other non-exempt person with less than $5 million in gross receipts for the credit tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the 5-tax-year period ending with the credit tax year—and checks the box on Section D, Line 33a to elect to claim a portion of its research credit as a payroll tax credit (up to $500,000 on Line 34); a QSB that does not check the box on Line 33a is not exempt under this provision. Under the Small-Filer QRE and Gross Receipts Exemption, the taxpayer is exempt if its total QREs determined at the controlled group level on Section F, Line 48 are $1.5 million or less, its average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less (determined at the controlled group level under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph 448(c)(3)(A)), and the taxpayer is claiming the research credit on a timely filed original return.

Third, with respect to The "80%/Top 50" Reporting Cap and Aggregate Reporting, non-exempt filers are not required to itemize every single business component if they have more than 50 components or a long tail of minor projects. Instead, filers required to complete Section G must itemize business components in descending order of total QREs per component until they have reported at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components ("80%/Top 50"). Controlled groups generally determine the 80%/Top 50 components at the controlled group level, whereas controlled group members filing separate tax returns report only their own QREs in Section F and itemize at least 80% of their own individual member QREs across no more than 50 of their own business components (per the IRS clarification issued June 18, 2025 and incorporated into the December 2025 instructions). Any remaining business components beyond the 80%/Top 50 are reported on a single summary line by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) (leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank) and entering the applicable aggregate dollar amounts in Columns 50 through 56. Additionally, eligible large taxpayers (assets of $10,000,000 or more following U.S. GAAP Certified Audited Financial Statements) that elect the ASC 730 Directive on Section E, Line 41 enter "ASC 730 Directive" on a single line in Column 49(c) and report their Appendix B (Column A) totals directly in Columns 53 through 56 without breaking out Columns 50–52; this single entry is not counted toward the 50-component limit, and if it accounts for at least 80% of total QREs on Line 48, no additional business components need to be itemized. Taxpayers using statistical sampling under Revenue Procedure 2011-42 must still report the 80%/Top 50 business components irrespective of which components were sampled, append the word "sample" to sampled component identifiers in Column 49(c), and attach their sampling plan as Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf.

Fourth, with respect to Research Credit Claims on Amended Returns and Refund Claims, when claiming a new or increased Section 41 research credit on an amended return (e.g., Form 1120-X or Form 1040-X) or an Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR), taxpayers must satisfy the specificity requirements under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1), IRM 4.46.3.7.6, and IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16), and must complete Column 49(f) of Section G (attaching Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf and, if applicable, Form6765Study.pdf when e-filing). While the IRS initially required five items of information under Interim Guidance LB&I-04-1222-0026 for refund claims postmarked prior to June 18, 2024, the IRS waived two items effective for claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024—specifically waiving the initial filing requirement to submit (1) the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and (2) the information each individual sought to discover (though both items may still be requested if the claim is selected for examination, and Column 49(f) remains required when completing Section G on an amended return). Consequently, under IRM 4.46.3.7.6 and IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16), a valid refund claim postmarked on or after June 18, 2024 must provide at minimum three items of information accompanied by a declaration signed under penalties of perjury: (1) identify all business components to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that year, (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed (describing what the taxpayer did and how they did it, without merely restating statutory or regulatory language), and (3) provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which is satisfied by properly completing Form 6765). Furthermore, the IRS extended the 45-day transition period to perfect deficient research credit refund claims—first through January 10, 2026 (via LB&I-04-0125-0001 on November 25, 2024) and subsequently through January 10, 2027 (via IR-2025-99 on October 1, 2025 and IRM Procedural Update ts-21-0126-0032 on January 2, 2026)—during which taxpayers notified of a deficient claim via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428 are granted 45 days to perfect the submission before the IRS issues a final determination of no consideration via Letter 6424C or Letter 6430.

Captures in-house wages for actual conduct of qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1) for each 80%/Top 50 and aggregate business component.
Direct supervision wages for qualified services
Captures in-house wages for immediate first-line supervision of qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) for each 80%/Top 50 and aggregate business component.
Direct support wages for qualified services

Core Direct Support reporting field: Captures in-house wages for services directly supporting researchers or first-line supervisors under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) for each 80%/Top 50 and aggregate business component.
Total qualified wages (add line 50, line 51, and line 52)
Sums Direct Research (Col. 50), Direct Supervision (Col. 51), and Direct Support (Col. 52) wages for each component; total across all rows transfers to Section F, Line 42.

body.text: 5. Institutionalizing Compliance, Audit Defense, and Pre-Filing IRS Resolution
Internal Controls, Supervisory Training, and Job Descriptions Versus Actual Duties

Because Section G of Form 6765 disaggregates qualified wages into Direct Research (Column 50), Direct Supervision (Column 51), and Direct Support (Column 52) by business component, taxpayers can no longer rely on undifferentiated departmental wage pools. Institutionalizing a defensible Direct Support compliance program requires four operational controls grounded in IRS examination procedures:

items: Regulatory Mapping and R&D Tax Policy Manual: Organizations should establish a written R&D Tax Policy Manual that maps every internal support role (technicians, machinists, lab workers, data clerks, specialized IT) against the explicit inclusion and exclusion examples of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3).

Project-Linked Time Capture Consistent with Books and Records: Because Column 49(c) of Form 6765 requires a business component name or unique alphanumeric identifier consistent with the taxpayer's books and records, ERP and timekeeping systems should assign unique project codes to each business component and require support staff to log hours separately between experimental prototype or testing support (qualified Direct Support) and commercial production or general maintenance (excluded).

First-Line Supervisory Review and Technical Interviews: Since Direct Support encompasses services supporting both active researchers and their first-line supervisors under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)(i)–(ii), first-line R&D managers are best positioned to verify whether support tasks had a direct nexus to a specific experiment before payroll and QRE workpapers are finalized.

Job Descriptions Versus Actual Duties Caveat: While aligning job descriptions with actual duties helps avoid superficial red flags during initial IRS screening (since the IRS ATG notes that initial Information Document Requests (IDRs) request employee job titles and job descriptions, and instructs examiners to focus audit resources on employees whose job descriptions suggest administrative, manufacturing, or marketing activities), taxpayers must recognize that updating a job description is never sufficient by itself. The IRS ATG states explicitly: "Determinations as to whether an employee is (or is not) engaged in qualified services should not be based solely on job descriptions or titles. Credit eligibility is based solely upon what an employee actually does, or does not, do during a specific time period".

body.text: Proactive IRS Resolution Pathways: Correcting the PLR Versus PFA Distinction

First, practitioners must distinguish Tax Credit Eligibility (IRC § 41) from Expense Deductibility (IRC § 174A). Qualifying Direct Support wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) determines whether those wages are eligible for the IRC § 41 research tax credit—a dollar-for-dollar reduction of tax liability. Deductibility or capitalization of domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures is governed separately by IRC § 174A, which was added to the Internal Revenue Code by Public Law 119-21 (commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or OBBBA) and permits taxpayers to immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A(a) (or elect to capitalize and amortize them ratably over not less than 60 months under IRC § 174A(c), following transition procedures in Revenue Procedure 2025-28) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, replacing the mandatory 5-year domestic amortization under IRC § 174 that applied for tax years 2022 through 2024 (while foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization). Furthermore, under IRC § 280C(c) (as amended by OBBBA § 70302(b)(2)(B)), taxpayers must either reduce their domestic IRC § 174A deduction or capital account charge by the full research credit claimed (attaching Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf when e-filing) or elect the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2) on Form 6765, Item A (multiplying the credit by 79%—which equals a 15.8% net regular credit rate on Line 13 or 79% of the ASC on Line 26).

Second, a Private Letter Ruling (PLR) is ordinarily unavailable for factual Direct Support determinations. Under Revenue Procedure 2026-1 (2026-1 I.R.B. 1, superseding Revenue Procedure 2025-1) and IRM 4.30.1, the IRS Associate Chief Counsel issues PLRs to interpret and apply tax law on unresolved questions of law involving proposed transactions or completed transactions prior to return filing. Under Section 6.02 of Revenue Procedure 2026-1, however, the Service ordinarily will not issue a letter ruling in certain areas because of the factual nature of the problem. Whether a specific employee's activities factually constitute Direct Support of qualified research under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) is an inherently factual determination governed by well-established regulations; consequently, IRM 4.30.1.1(3) explicitly states that PFAs are strictly for issues that are factual in nature and governed by well-established law, whereas issues involving unresolved questions of law are resolved through the PLR process.

Third, Pre-Filing Agreements (PFAs) and Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreements (RCRAs) are the designated administrative vehicles for factual and recordkeeping certainty, subject to strict eligibility and fee constraints. Under Revenue Procedure 2016-30 (2016-21 I.R.B. 981) and IRM 4.30.1, taxpayers under the jurisdiction of the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Division may apply for a PFA to examine and resolve specific factual issues or methodologies used to determine the appropriate amount of a credit governed by well-established law for a completed transaction or period before the tax return is filed (covering the current taxable year, any prior taxable year for which the original return is not yet due and not yet filed, and methodology agreements for up to four future taxable years). A resolved PFA for a current or prior unfiled year is memorialized as a closing agreement under IRC § 7121, whereas agreements covering future taxable years (or prior taxable years whose returns are not yet due) are executed as non-statutory agreements under Revenue Procedure 2016-30 Section 7.02(2) that function as binding contracts conditioned on stated assumptions. Although the IRS has accepted PFAs to determine the proper amount of QREs and research credits under IRC § 41, participating taxpayers selected for the PFA program must pay a substantial non-refundable user fee within 15 business days via Pay.gov—set in IRM 4.30.1.3(7.3) at $181,500 per separate and distinct issue for requests received after February 1, 2020 (subject to updates in the annual first Revenue Procedure). Alternatively, as detailed in IRS ATG Section 7, large business taxpayers seeking prospective agreement specifically on what documentation and time-tracking records the IRS will accept to substantiate research credits in future tax years can enter into a Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreement (RCRA) pursuant to Notice 2004-11 (2004-6 I.R.B.). While an RCRA does not resolve whether underlying activities satisfy IRC § 41(d), maintaining the agreed-upon records under an RCRA generally eliminates audit disallowance for lack of substantiation.
Comprehensive Direct Support Compliance Checklist

cells: Configure payroll and QRE workpapers to segregate qualified employee wages into three distinct buckets per business component: Direct Research (Col. 50), Direct Supervision (Col. 51), and Direct Support (Col. 52).
Prevents commingling of support and supervisory wages; ensures readiness for mandatory post-2025 Section G filing.
Assign a unique project name or alphanumeric identifier to each business component in timekeeping and ERP records that matches the identifier reported in Form 6765 Section G, Column 49(c).
IRC § 41(d)(2)(A); Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2025), Col. 49(c); IRS RCCATG.
Establishes the mandatory cost-to-component nexus and satisfies the 80%/Top 50 business component reporting rules.

Record contemporaneous task descriptions linking support hours to specific experimental activities (e.g., prototype machining, lab equipment cleaning, test data compilation) and excluding G&A or commercial production.
Overcomes IRS audit scrutiny of support and manufacturing job titles by proving what the employee actually did during the period.
Compute each employee's ratio of total qualified service hours (Research + Supervision + Support) to total hours worked; apply 100% wage inclusion only where the ratio is at least 80%.
Prevents improper 100% wage claims for hybrid support staff below 80% while capturing the full statutory benefit for staff at or above 80%.

Restrict base wage figures strictly to taxable W-2 wages under IRC § 3401(a); remove non-taxable fringe benefits and any wages used to compute the IRC § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit; disclose officer wages on Line 38.
Eliminates computational errors on W-2 wage inclusions and satisfies Section E officer wage disclosure.
